summary_html: CPS **screens out** a report (no investigation) or closes as **unfounded** after minimal review. Federal law (CAPTA) conditions funding on operating screening criteria and recordkeeping; federal reviews (CFSR) assess decision quality. In Alabama the age of majority is 19 (Ala. Code § 26-1-1), and for child abuse and neglect reporting a "child" is a person under 18, or a person under 19 who is in need of protective services and does not qualify for adult protective services (Ala. Code § 26-14-1(3)). If a report is marked **indicated**, the full § 26-14-7.1 hearing (counsel, witnesses, cross-examination, subpoenas, an impartial hearing officer) is available only to a person connected with a facility, agency, or home that cares for and controls children; everyone else, including a parent investigated at home, receives the DHR administrative record review, which DHR describes as "provided for those persons not entitled to a hearing" and for which the DHR review page states no deadline (dhr.alabama.gov/child-protective-services/child-abuse-neglect-administrative-reviews).

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.holding: The Court held that a DHR service supervisor who, on receiving an intake report flagged for an immediate response, had no investigator available and instead confirmed the injured child would remain in the hospital over the weekend exercised protected supervisory judgment and was entitled to State-agent immunity.
key_cases.relevance: Delay or deviation at the screening stage is measured against the DHR manual's response-time criteria.
key_cases.quote: The materials before us support a finding that Sumerlin did not ignore her responsibility; rather, she exercised her judgment in her supervisory capacity to deal with exigent circumstances.

key_cases.holding: The Court denied State-agent immunity to the CA/N investigator, who never made the home visit required by Ala. Admin. Code r. 660-5-34-.05(1)(b), and to the ongoing worker, who ignored her supervisor's binding written instructions, but granted immunity to the two supervisors whose duties involved judgment.
key_cases.relevance: An assessment closed without the required home visit cannot support a protected screening judgment.
key_cases.quote: because Watson has not submitted substantial evidence indicating that she complied with subsection (b), Watson has not demonstrated that she is entitled to State-agent immunity

key_cases.holding: The Court restated the rule governing State-agent immunity into five categories of protected conduct subject to two exceptions - conduct that federal or state law requires otherwise, and conduct that is willful, malicious, fraudulent, in bad faith, beyond authority or under a mistaken interpretation of law - and held that university physicians treating a student fell within no protected category and so were not immune.
key_cases.relevance: A screening or closure decision is protected only if it is genuine judgment within a Cranman category and free of bad faith.
key_cases.quote: when the State agent acts willfully, maliciously, fraudulently, in bad faith, beyond his or her authority, or under a mistaken interpretation of the law

key_cases.case_name: Gowens v. Tys. S. ex rel. Davis
key_cases.holding: The Court held that a DHR investigator was not protected by Ala. Code 26-14-9, which covers reporting rather than investigating, and was not entitled to Cranman State-agent immunity because the DHR Manual's investigation standards required him to verify from an outside source how many children were in the household and to interview them, leaving him no judgment to exercise; it also held he owed the uninterviewed children a duty.
key_cases.relevance: An investigation closed without verifying who actually lives in the home is not a protected exercise of screening judgment.
key_cases.quote: The mandates of the DHR Manual in this regard are precisely the sort of "detailed rules or regulations" that State agents cannot ignore, except at their peril.
